result.summary: Achilles rages through the Trojans until Phoebus Apollo shoots him in the ankle; he kills several more men and dies. Aias and Odysseus save his body, and the Greeks, Briseis, Thetis, the Nereids and the Muses mourn him. He is burned on a great pyre, his bones are buried by the Hellespont, and Poseidon promises him an island.

scenes.title: Apollo Strikes Achilles Down
scenes.summary: Antilochus is buried, and Achilles storms against Troy until Phoebus warns him off. Achilles defies the god and is shot in the ankle.
scenes.stakes: Achilles risks his life by defying a god, and the Trojans risk the fall of their city.

scenes.title: Achilles Falls, Draws the Arrow
scenes.summary: Achilles falls, guesses Apollo shot him, and pulls out the shaft. The wind carries the arrow back to Apollo.

scenes.title: Hera Rebukes Phoebus
scenes.summary: On Olympus Hera angrily reproaches Phoebus for killing Achilles. He sits ashamed and silent.
scenes.stakes: Phoebus faces the anger of Hera and the Immortals.

scenes.title: Achilles' Last Stand
scenes.summary: Wounded, Achilles kills several Trojans, then shouts a last threat and dies. The Trojans stare at him in fear.

scenes.title: Battle Over the Body
scenes.summary: Paris urges the Trojans to drag off the corpse. Aias, Odysseus and the Greeks fight them off, and Aias wounds Paris with a stone and drives the Trojans into the city.
scenes.stakes: Achilles' body could be dragged off and mutilated by the Trojans.

scenes.title: Greeks Mourn at the Ships
scenes.summary: The corpse is carried to the tents, and Aias, Phoenix and Agamemnon lament.
scenes.stakes: The Greeks fear defeat without Achilles.

scenes.title: Washing the Body; Briseis Laments
scenes.summary: Nestor calls for the body to be washed. Athena preserves it, and Briseis mourns.
scenes.stakes: Briseis fears slavery under a new master.

scenes.title: Nereids and Muses Mourn
scenes.summary: Thetis, the Nereids and the Muses come to mourn, and Calliope urges Thetis to bear her grief. The Greeks weep for many days.
scenes.stakes: Thetis fears she has lost her son and thinks of angering Zeus.

scenes.title: The Pyre and the Barrow
scenes.summary: Achilles is burned on a great pyre fanned by the winds sent by Aeolus. His bones are buried in a barrow, and his immortal horses stay and mourn.

scenes.title: Poseidon Consoles Thetis
scenes.summary: Poseidon promises Thetis that Achilles will live on as a god on an island in the Euxine Sea. The Greeks go back to the ships, and the Muses and Nereids depart.

notable_quotes.reason: Achilles recalls his mother's prophecy that he would die by Apollo's arrows at the Scaean Gates.
Aias's bleak maxim that the gods grant no perfect happiness to mortals.

analysis.text: Achilles' death shows fate and the gods overriding even the greatest hero's pride. The mourning that follows shows the cost of war on both sides.
The funeral, with offerings, slain victims, shorn hair and a barrow on the shore, follows heroic burial customs like those in Homer's Iliad. The poem fills in events the Iliad leaves out.

legacy.text: Achilles' vulnerable heel, his ankle shot by Apollo, gave us the phrase 'Achilles' heel' and the name of the Achilles tendon.

fun_facts.text: This poem is by Quintus of Smyrna, a Greek poet of the 3rd or 4th century AD, and is also called the Posthomerica. It continues the story from the end of the Iliad.

language_notes.text: Antilochus, Nestor's son, was killed earlier by Memnon while protecting his father; the Pylians are Nestor's people, from Pylos.
"Aeacus' son" means Peleus' son Achilles in a roundabout way: Achilles' father Peleus was himself a son of Aeacus, so strictly Achilles is Aeacus' grandson.
A long conditional: Achilles would have destroyed Troy "but" Phoebus intervened. "Burg" means fortified town; "Danaans" means Greeks.
"Beseems not" means "it is not fitting"; "abase thy pride" means humble you.
"Recked" means heeded or cared about; he paid the god no heed.
Refers to an earlier episode in which Apollo, disguised, lured Achilles away from the fight so Hector escaped death.
Phoebus says not even Zeus (Jove's Greek name) could save Achilles, signalling that the Fates have already decided his end.
"Smit" is an archaic past participle of smite: struck. The image is a tower toppled when an earthquake opens the ground and winds burst out.
"Thews" means muscles or bodily strength; "thews of brass" means a body as strong as bronze.
"Dastards" are cowards, especially those who attack unfairly.
"Danaans" is a name for the Greeks, from Danaus, a legendary ancestor.
Achilles recalls his mother Thetis's prophecy that he would die at Troy, killed by Apollo's arrows near the Scaean Gates.
"It beseemed not" means it was not fitting; a divine weapon could not be left lying among mortals.
"Bride of Zeus" is a poetic title for Hera, Zeus's wife and queen of the gods; "Upbraided" means scolded.
"Spousals" means the wedding celebration of Peleus and Thetis.
Phoebus (Apollo) once served the Trojan king Laomedon as a herdsman, tending his cattle ("kine"), after being punished by Zeus. Laomedon later cheated him of his wages.
"Wit-bereft" means robbed of wits, senseless.
Achilles' son Neoptolemus is being brought from Scyros, where he was raised, to fight at Troy. "Aeacus' son" is Peleus, but here it means Achilles, grandson of Aeacus.
"I ween" means I think or I suppose; "bane" means destroyer.
"Nereid" is a sea-nymph, daughter of Nereus; here it refers to Thetis, Achilles' mother.
"Fain" means gladly or willingly.
"Forgat" is an archaic past tense of "forget"; the line says Achilles had not yet forgotten war's fury.
"Peleides" is a patronymic meaning "son of Peleus," a name for Achilles.
"God-envenomed wound" refers to the arrow guided by Apollo into Achilles' heel, poisoned with Hydra's venom in some tellings.
"Avenging Spirits" are the Furies-like powers of vengeance that Achilles says will punish the Trojans after his death.
"Cravens" means cowards; "Dardan" means Trojan, from Dardanus, an ancestor of the Trojans.
"Aweless" means fearless, not moved by awe or dread.
"Beetling" describes a cliff that overhangs or juts out threateningly.
"Hale" means drag or haul by force; Paris proposes dragging Achilles' body to Troy behind Hector's horses.
"Eld" is old age; the old men are kept inside the walls by their age.
"Recking naught" means paying no heed; "fane" is a temple.
"I wot" means "I know"; archaic first-person form.
Glaucus's grandfather Bellerophon was a guest-friend of Aias's ancestors; Tydeus' son (Diomedes) once exchanged armour with Glaucus rather than fight him, in the Iliad.
Panaceia's name is placed in apostrophic exclamation, lamenting that she never saw her son again.
"Bolt of death" here means the thrown stone, not an arrow.
"Unstripped of arms" means the dead Trojans were not yet despoiled of their armour.
Tityos, a giant, tried to assault Leto, mother of Apollo and Artemis, on her way to Pytho (Delphi); Apollo shot him down. His vast body covering ground is the comparison.
"Aeacus' son" is Achilles; the poem uses this patronymic for Peleus' son, since Aeacus was Peleus' father, so Achilles is his grandson.
Ares was struck down by Athena ("She of the Mighty Father", daughter of Zeus), who hurled a huge stone at him in the Trojan war.
"Father's brother's son" means cousin: Aias' father Telamon and Peleus were brothers. "God-stricken" means killed by a god.
"Eld" is an old word for old age.
Phoenix fled his homeland after a quarrel with his father, then was received by Peleus, who made him ruler of the Dolopians.
Atreides means 'son of Atreus', i.e. Agamemnon. Nestor is called Neleus' son in the same way.
Aweless means fearless or not awe-struck; here it is an epithet for Aeacus, Achilles' grandfather.
Corse is an old word for corpse; vesture means clothing.
The Trito-born is Athena (Minerva in some translations), said to be born near Lake Triton or from the river of that name.
Ambrosia is the food or perfume of the gods; it preserves flesh from decay. Taintless means uncorrupted.
Refers to Achilles' earlier raids, including Lemnos and Thebes, the city of Eetion, where captive women were taken.
Couchmate means concubine or bedfellow; weals are raised welts left by blows.
Achaean is another name for Greek. Briseis fears being given as a slave to a new master in Sparta or Argos.
"Upringing" means rising up; the wail of the Greeks rises over the sea to the sea-nymphs below.
"Nereus' Daughters" are the Nereids, sea-nymphs, of whom Thetis is one.
"Overpalled" means covered as with a pall or cloak; "mantles" are cloaks.
"Corse" is an old word for corpse.
"Rosy-vestured Dawn" refers to Eos, the goddess of dawn, who is also named elsewhere in the poem.
Axius is a river-god whose grandson Asteropaeus was killed by Achilles; Thetis imagines even he can now stop his anger.
"Eld" means old age; the man is Peleus, a mortal.
Thetis recalls shape-shifting to escape marriage with Peleus, who held on until she yielded.
"Recks not" means does not care about or heed.
Peleides means 'son of Peleus', a patronymic for Achilles. Argives is a common name for the Greeks.
Atreus' sons are Agamemnon and Menelaus, the Greek commanders.
Shore is the old past tense of 'shear': the Myrmidons cut off their hair as a sign of mourning.
'Rich blood of the grape' is a poetic phrase for wine.
'Bale' means funeral fire; 'compassed' means encircled.
'The Fire-god's madding breath' means the flames, driven into a frenzy by the winds; the Fire-god is Hephaestus, here standing for fire itself.
'Ravined up' means devoured greedily.
A hecatomb is a great sacrifice of many animals, originally a hundred.
Nards are fragrant ointments made from spikenard; kine are cattle.
A barrow is a burial mound; a foreland is a headland.
Earth-shaker is a standard epithet of Poseidon, god of the sea and earthquakes.

context_notes.text: Simois and Xanthus are the two rivers of the Trojan plain; Xanthus is also called Scamander.
Phoebus Apollo, god of archery, plague and prophecy, favoured Troy and was the divine power behind Achilles' death.
Achilles' vulnerable heel or ankle is the famous spot where he is fatally wounded; here the arrow strikes it.
Aeacus was Achilles' grandfather, so Achilles is called "Aeacus' son" by descent, as a grandson would be.
The Scaean Gates were the main gate of Troy's walls, a landmark in the war.
Zeus' threshold is the entrance to the king of the gods' home on Olympus; Apollo, god of archery, receives his arrow back there.
Olympus was the home of the gods, who watch the Trojan War from there, each taking a side.
Phoebus Apollo killed Achilles at Troy, guiding Paris's arrow. Hera sided with the Greeks (Danaans) and felt this keenly.
Achilles was close to the gods by descent: his father Peleus was a mortal favored by them, and his mother Thetis was a sea goddess.
Orythaon is a Trojan fighter, here called a comrade of Hector, the Trojan champion and Achilles' great enemy.
Hades is the underworld, where the souls of the dead go.
The "battle-helpers drawn from alien lands" are Troy's foreign allies, who came from other regions to fight for the city.
Achilles has just been killed; Hector, Paris' brother, was earlier slain by Achilles, whose horses Paris now uses.
Glaucus, Aeneas and Agenor are Trojan allies and champions; Glaucus leads the Lycians.
Aias (Ajax), son of Telamon, was Achilles' cousin and the greatest Greek warrior after him.
Laertes' son is Odysseus, the Greek known for cunning, fighting beside Aias to protect Achilles' body.
Hellespont is the strait by which the Greek ships lay, so the dead stretch from Troy to the Greek camp.
The Myrmidons were Achilles' own followers, from Phthia in Thessaly.
Achilles was killed by an arrow shot by Paris, guided by Apollo. Greeks of the heroic ideal despised archery as unmanly.
Phoenix was Achilles' aged tutor and foster-father, sent with him to Troy by Peleus.
Agamemnon recalls that Zeus had promised he would sack Priam's city; Achilles' death makes it seem the promise has failed.
Nestor's son Antilochus was killed at Troy by Memnon, so Nestor knows grief personally.
Achilles' mother is the sea-goddess Thetis, which fits the sea-purple garment she gave him.
Briseis was Achilles' war-prize, whose seizure by Agamemnon caused the quarrel in the Iliad. Achilles' killing of her brothers is known from the Iliad.
Helicon is a mountain in Boeotia sacred to the Muses, goddesses of poetry, music and the arts.
Dawn's son Memnon had been killed by Achilles, so Thetis bitterly imagines Dawn rejoicing.
Calliope is the Muse of epic poetry, here speaking as a consoling elder sister.
Orpheus, son of Calliope, was the legendary singer whose music charmed nature; he was later killed by Thracian women.
Briseis was the captive woman Achilles was given as a prize; Agamemnon's taking of her began the quarrel in the Iliad.
Aeolus was the keeper of the winds, and Hermes was the gods' messenger.
The Wine-god is Dionysus and the Fire-god is Hephaestus, the divine smith. The vase was a gift to Thetis.
Achilles' immortal horses were Xanthus and Balius, whose mother was the harpy Podarge.
Neoptolemus was Achilles' son, raised on Scyros and soon to join the war at Troy.
The Euxine is the Black Sea. Achilles was worshipped as a hero on its island Leuke, 'White Island'.

literary_notes.text: Nestor's calm endurance is praised as wisdom, contrasting with Achilles' rage.
The narrator announces that Achilles himself is doomed to die that very day, preparing the climax.
The god's leap from Olympus is compared to a lion's spring, conveying predatory speed and menace.
The Fates are imagined as beings hovering around Achilles, making his defiance seem driven by destiny.
Phoebus calls Achilles sense-bereft for threatening a god, though Achilles' arrogance is what brings his doom.
Achilles' fall is compared to a tower struck in an earthquake, conveying his huge size and the shock of his collapse.
The narrator notes the threat "could not be fulfilled," showing Achilles' fury is already powerless against his fate.
Achilles' guess that Apollo shot him recalls the prophecy and signals that his death is certain.
The "shadow of coming doom" presents approaching death as a darkness falling over his heart.
Nature itself is described as attending the wedding song, with hills, rivers and forests coming to listen. This shows how great Apollo's music was.
Hera's exclamation addresses Phoebus directly in the heat of anger, making her rebuke feel immediate and passionate.
Hera asks how he will face Thetis, shaming Phoebus and implying that he has no defense.
Phoebus's silence and lowered eyes show his shame and the gods' fear of Hera's wrath, which even the Trojan-supporting gods must conceal their joy from.
Achilles is compared to a wounded lion ringed by fearful hunters, showing his undiminished courage and the danger he still poses.
His lance is called lightning, conveying its speed, brilliance and deadly force.
Trojans are like fawns trembling at a lion's roar, reversing their earlier role as hunters and underlining Achilles' terrifying power.
His fall is likened to a mountain cliff collapsing, stressing his immense size and the finality of his death.
Sheep still fearing a slain beast show that Achilles' dread outlasts his life, ending the scene with irony and awe.
Troy's women are compared to enraged panthers and lionesses around a hunter, showing their fury at Achilles.
Aias ignoring the Trojan assault is likened to a honey-thief unmoved by angry bees, stressing their futility.
Aias calls the Trojan helpers worthless flies, belittling them as pests around a corpse.
Glaucus's fall onto Achilles is compared to a sapling falling on a mountain oak, contrasting weak and mighty.
Slain men are likened to autumn leaves blown down, evoking waste and the passing of life.
Fleeing Trojans are like vultures scared by an eagle, casting Aias as the superior predator.
Terror is described as a cloak the Trojans wear, making their fear visible.
Fallen warriors are compared to cut corn, while the farmer's joy contrasts with the grim scene, making slaughter look like harvest.
The Greeks' wailing is likened to the cries of a sacked city, showing how total their loss feels.
Achilles is praised as kind and courteous, strikingly different from his usual wrath and softening his heroic image.
The Trojans' fear of Achilles is likened to sheep fearing a lion, stressing his terrifying power.
The ships echo and the air sighs and sobs, so the whole landscape seems to join the mourning.
Waves battering the shore illustrate the endless, crashing surge of the Greeks' grief, closing the scene.
Achilles is compared to a sleeper, showing Athena's miracle that makes death look like life.
Red blood on pale skin is compared to crimson dripping on milk, making her grief vivid and painful to see.
Briseis calls Achilles her day, sunlight and life, showing how completely he sustained her.
Her tears are compared to water trickling from a frozen rock, suggesting grief that melts slowly but does not stop.
The nymphs' cry is compared to cranes' calls that warn of a coming storm, adding ominous tone.
Tears fall like rain, showing the scale of the goddesses' grief.
Even armour, tents and ships are wet with tears, exaggerating the army's mourning.
Fate is a powerful figure who hovers over people and disregards even the gods.
Night is a dark-robed woman who floats up the sky bringing sleep as a gift.
Dawn laughs triumphantly as she rises, contrasting with the mourners' sorrow.
Sea, land and clouds roar and crash as the winds pass, so nature itself seems to take part in the funeral.
The winds swooping like a charging host gives the gale the force of an army attacking.
His bones are like those of a Giant and lie apart from all the other remains, which shows his superhuman greatness even in death.
The immortal horses mourn like men, which deepens the sense of loss and shows how widely Achilles was loved.
Poseidon's departure is likened to a wind-breath, which shows how swiftly and unseen a god moves.
